items.originalTitle: OpenAI still has a WebRTC Problem
items.summary:
OpenAI continues to struggle with WebRTC's limitations in voice AI applications, where its design for real-time human communication causes problems like dropped audio packets and latency during network disruptions. WebRTC's aggressive packet dropping to minimize latency leads to wasted tokens or inaccurate AI responses when users experience connectivity issues such as moving out of Wi-Fi range or cellular dead zones.

The core issue is that WebRTC prioritizes low latency for human conversations, disabling audio retransmissions by default to avoid delays and bursts of audio that degrade user experience. However, voice AI systems operate faster than real-time and can tolerate retransmissions without user impact, suggesting that WebRTC's human-centric design is ill-suited for AI voice agents. The article argues for retransmission strategies that ensure all audio packets arrive before AI processing, improving accuracy and user experience in voice AI products.

items.title: Report: AI platforms turn skilled jobs into low-paid gig work with variable rates and limited worker protections [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AI isn't replacing your job. It's turning it into low-paid gig work
items.summary:
AI-driven platforms like Scale AI and Outlier are recruiting professionals such as physicians, lawyers, and Ph.D.s to perform tasks like data annotation and model evaluation, often paying widely varying rates based on location and credentials. These platforms initially offer higher pay to build a workforce but then reduce rates and shift tasks geographically, leaving many workers with unstable and low incomes.

Interviews with workers in countries like Venezuela reveal how economic crises and platform practices have pushed educated individuals into precarious gig work, with earnings fluctuating and platforms sometimes freezing accounts without notice. The system reflects a form of digital extractivism, where value is extracted from workers globally under terms controlled by the platform, often with limited transparency or recourse.

This shift raises concerns about the sustainability and fairness of AI-related gig work, as well as the broader implications for labor markets where highly skilled professionals may face diminishing pay and job security while supporting AI development.

items.title: Researchers audit AI-agent security benchmark AgentDojo, find 11.9% of attacks missed and release .sova tool for reproducible verification [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Did the attack work? Auditing AI-agent security benchmark verdicts
items.summary:
Researchers audited the AI-agent security benchmark AgentDojo by re-running attacks on 24 models from eight developers and comparing verdicts against actual agent actions. They found that while the benchmark agreed with audit results on 97.7% of non-crashing runs, it missed 11.9% of attacks where agents executed decisive attacker actions, such as paying the attacker. The team released .sova, an open-source tool and record format that audits verdicts, re-runs findings on chosen models, and seals evidence for offline verification against published checksums.

The audit involved 19,381 published runs and identified issues such as false positives where warnings were counted as attacks and inconsistent attack recurrence across model versions. Pre-registered rules for stopping attacks showed mixed success across different models. The study highlights challenges in reliably benchmarking AI-agent security and provides tools to improve transparency and reproducibility in evaluating AI vulnerabilities.

items.originalSummary:
Today is a major milestone for Anthropic. The five-year-old maker of Claude beat its archrival OpenAI to the public markets, and many of its employees are going to become millionaires, if not billionaires, when the company starts to trade later today. The big question is what today means for Anthropic’s future.

Before we get to that, let’s set the scene. Anthropic priced the offering at $83 a share, well  above its preliminary pricing range, valuing the company at about $1.5 trillion. Chances are the stock will trade significantly higher when it opens later Thursday. For employees looking to cash in, they’ll need the stock to stay higher for a while. While they can sell up to 10% of their shares on the first day of trading, they can’t sell more until the company reports its full-year 2026 earnings early next year.

Assuming the stock doesn’t tank, the sudden influx of money will help Anthropic employees buy houses and donate a big chunk of their newfound wealth to causes like shrimp welfare. Counterintuitively, though, it may also lead them to leave the very company that brought them the wealth in the first place.

You may think that employees at a company as philosophically driven as Anthropic are as bought in as the cofounders and in it for the long haul. That’s not necessarily true. At the end of the day, many of the employees, especially those who have joined more recently from big tech companies, might not be drinking the Kool-Aid as much as just trying to make a quick buck.

items.summary:
Architect Labs has developed Frostbite, a general-purpose CPU architecture designed and verified autonomously by AI systems, which achieves a 4.59x improvement in performance-per-watt compared to a modern superscalar CPU. Frostbite leverages interaction nets, a computational model where every step is local and dependencies are explicit, enabling efficient parallelism and reduced power consumption by eliminating shared mutable state and complex cache coherence.

The AI systems iterated across the entire hardware stack, including compiler, ISA, microarchitecture, and verification, discovering novel architectural primitives and runtime features that would be difficult for humans to design. This approach allowed the team to overcome the long-standing stagnation in single-core CPU performance and suggests that AI-driven co-design could lead to fundamental shifts in various chip classes, from datacenter CPUs to AI accelerators and networking hardware.

items.originalTitle: China’s Moonshot AI Scraps $150 Million Deal to Access Nvidia Chips in Indonesia
items.summary:
Moonshot AI, the Beijing-based developer of the Kimi models, has scrapped a $150 million deal to access Nvidia Blackwell chips through a data center in Indonesia, after the U.S. this week announced a rule to restrict Chinese companies from accessing advanced chips remotely, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter.

Moonshot signed the contract with a Southeast Asian neocloud to rent access to a sizable cluster of Blackwell Ultra B300 chips, starting from as early as next year, the people said. The B300 is one of Nvidia’s most powerful AI chips, and is barred by the U.S. government from sale to China. Chinese companies were able to access restricted Nvidia chips from data centers outside of the country, a loophole that was plugged by the rule released by the U.S. Commerce Department this week.
